title: Devout Christians boast great family lives. Lukewarm ones fare worse than the non-religious | Institute for Family Studies
gist: A Washington Examiner op-ed teaser (via IFS) by Jane Lankes Smith, per its title: devout Christians have strong family lives while lukewarm or nominal ones fare worse than the non-religious. The excerpt only sets up the premise that nominal affiliation is assumed better than none; the finding itself is in the headline.

insights.claim: Devout Christians report strong family lives, while lukewarm (nominal) Christians fare worse on family outcomes than the non-religious, according to the article's headline.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Intensity of religious practice, not mere affiliation, appears to drive family outcomes; watch religiosity polarization.
insights.locator: Devout Christians boast great family lives. Lukewarm ones fare worse than the non-religious

insights.claim: Religious 'Nones' (atheists, agnostics, 'nothing in particular') have risen steadily in America since the early 1990s and tend to have lower social support and worse psychological well-being.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Secularization is a durable demographic trend linked to social-support deficits.

insights.claim: Conventional assumption holds that nominal affiliation is better than none, since nominal affiliates often keep theological convictions, pass on a Christian identity, volunteer more than lifelong secular people, and may later become active members.

insights.so_what: This is the consensus view the article sets up to challenge.
